clinicalPearls: Family of mesenchymal tumours built from perivascular epithelioid cells that characteristically co-express melanocytic markers (HMB-45, Melan-A, MITF) and smooth muscle markers (smooth muscle actin, desmin).
The family includes angiomyolipoma, pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis, clear cell sugar tumour of the lung and PEComa not otherwise specified of soft tissue and viscera.
Strong association with the tuberous sclerosis complex through loss of TSC1 or TSC2 and consequent activation of the mTOR pathway.
A biologically distinct subset is driven by TFE3 gene fusions; these arise in younger patients, lack a tuberous sclerosis association and show strong nuclear TFE3 staining with alveolar architecture.
There is a female predominance, and common sites include the uterus, retroperitoneum, gastrointestinal tract and soft tissue.
Malignant potential is stratified using features such as large size, infiltrative margins, high nuclear grade, high mitotic rate, necrosis and vascular invasion.
mTOR inhibitors (for example sirolimus and everolimus) are effective in advanced or malignant disease, reflecting the underlying pathway activation.
Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice for localised tumours.
reference.pathophysiology: Perivascular epithelioid cell tumours arise from the perivascular epithelioid cell, a cell type with no clear normal tissue counterpart that shows dual melanocytic and smooth muscle differentiation and is typically arranged around thin-walled blood vessels with clear to granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Most cases are underpinned by biallelic inactivation of TSC1 or TSC2, which releases mTOR complex 1 from inhibition and drives cell growth and proliferation; this molecular basis links the sporadic tumours to the lesions of the tuberous sclerosis complex, such as renal angiomyolipoma and pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis. A separate group is defined by fusions involving the TFE3 transcription factor gene, which activate a distinct transcriptional programme, occur in younger patients without tuberous sclerosis, and show strong nuclear TFE3 expression. The dual immunophenotype — positivity for HMB-45, Melan-A and MITF alongside smooth muscle actin and desmin — is the diagnostic hallmark and reflects this hybrid differentiation. Behaviour ranges from benign to overtly malignant, and because mTOR signalling is central to the tuberous-sclerosis-associated lesions these tumours are frequently responsive to mTOR inhibition even in the metastatic setting.
additionalDifferentials: Alveolar soft part sarcoma, given the TFE3 overlap
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) to characterise the lesion and assess extent
Histopathology with an immunohistochemical panel including HMB-45, Melan-A, smooth muscle actin, desmin and TFE3
Molecular testing for TFE3 rearrangement and TSC1/TSC2 status
Clinical and genetic assessment for the tuberous sclerosis complex when suggested by other features
Staging imaging including the chest when malignant features are present
Dedicated renal imaging where angiomyolipoma is suspected
redFlags: Large, rapidly growing or retroperitoneal tumours with infiltrative margins
High mitotic activity, marked atypia or coagulative necrosis on histology
Multiple lesions or other stigmata of the tuberous sclerosis complex
Acute retroperitoneal haemorrhage from a renal angiomyolipoma (Wunderlich syndrome)
reference.prognosis: Benign and small tumours excised completely have an excellent prognosis, whereas malignant perivascular epithelioid cell tumours can metastasise to lung, liver and bone and carry a guarded outlook. Responsiveness to mTOR inhibitors has improved outcomes in advanced disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking the tumour for melanoma because of HMB-45 and Melan-A positivity
Underestimating malignant potential in visceral and retroperitoneal lesions
Failing to recognise an associated tuberous sclerosis complex
Not considering mTOR inhibitor therapy in advanced or malignant disease
